title: How I Write LinkedIn Posts That Get 100,000+ Views
speakers_and_attribution: The transcript presents one first-person speaker, contextually identified as Adam Robinson through his business references and personal examples. No interviewer or guest appears. Captions are automatic and not diarized, so attribution is contextual rather than independently verified. The product name captioned as “OurB2B” may be a transcription error; its spelling is not resolved here.
summary: Adam explains his LinkedIn writing process: research audience questions, adapt proven post structures, establish credibility in the hook, develop a specific pain into a useful takeaway, and finish with emotional resonance. He credits candid accounts of business difficulties and bounded polarizing opinions with helping posts spread. Personal examples include criticism of the BDR model and publishing Retention.com’s product-market-fit and churn problems despite executive objections. He connects content to website-visitor identification and outreach through a promoted product. His audience and ARR figures are self-reports, and the relationship between the two different ARR claims is unspecified.

key_learnings.claim: Adam advises writing for what the audience wants to read rather than optimizing directly for the algorithm. He argues that understanding readers’ actual difficulties produces more compelling content than polished wins and safe opinions.
key_learnings.speaker: Adam Robinson
key_learnings.caveat: His account of algorithm behavior and platform-independent effectiveness is a generalization, not evidence from a controlled comparison.

key_learnings.claim: He describes a productive range of polarization: familiar consensus attracts little attention, while excessively extreme claims undermine credibility. His preferred position draws strong agreement and substantive disagreement; he illustrates it with posts criticizing BDR-led SaaS sales.
key_learnings.speaker: Adam Robinson
key_learnings.caveat: He calls this the prolific zone. The explanation attributes virality to disagreement without supplying post analytics or proving that the underlying BDR critique applies universally.

key_learnings.claim: Adam believes candid disclosure of business problems resonates with people experiencing similar difficulties. He cites publishing Retention.com’s layoff, lost product-market fit, and prolonged churn problems, while acknowledging that founders with investors may have less freedom to disclose this much.
key_learnings.speaker: Adam Robinson
key_learnings.pillar: building in public; bootstrapping versus VC
key_learnings.caveat: The investor limitation is his practical judgment, not a universal prohibition. He does not establish that more disclosure always improves business outcomes.

key_learnings.claim: His topic-research workflow starts with questions people already have: review the strongest posts from two or three niche creators over the preceding 90 days, record high-engagement topics in a spreadsheet, then add questions surfaced through Gemini and relevant Reddit threads.
key_learnings.speaker: Adam Robinson
key_learnings.caveat: This is a recommended workflow, not evidence that engagement identifies buying intent. His description of Gemini’s search capabilities is unverified.

key_learnings.claim: He recommends spending two hours building a swipe file of hooks, formats, and endings, then applying those structures to original experiences and perspectives. Templates are useful while developing comfort and judgment; writers can stop relying on them once they understand what their audience responds to.
key_learnings.speaker: Adam Robinson
key_learnings.caveat: Supporting passages are 00:03:18–00:03:42 and 00:05:43–00:05:59, with other topics between them. He recommends borrowing structure while supplying one's own story; this does not establish an approved voice guide for Adam.

key_learnings.claim: Adam gives the hook one immediate job: persuade a reader to expand the post. He recommends establishing credibility and making a bold statement, assuming readers do not know the author. He says he uses specific numbers in almost every hook to establish that credibility.
key_learnings.speaker: Adam Robinson
key_learnings.caveat: The hook examples mix an illustrative CEO-interview claim with his own asserted bootstrapping result. Specificity alone does not validate a number, and no comparative performance data is supplied.

key_learnings.claim: He recommends a three-part body: describe a precise audience pain, offer a solution or reframing, and leave an actionable takeaway. He treats formatting as flexible, saying he usually uses bullets with two or three sentences beneath them but also uses numbered lists and paragraphs.
key_learnings.speaker: Adam Robinson
key_learnings.caveat: This is his writing framework and reported format preference, not a demonstrated requirement for all effective posts.

key_learnings.claim: Adam prefers endings that create an emotional response over generic requests for comments. His example encourages bootstrappers to persist through the disadvantages of being small and acknowledges that success can require both time and luck.
key_learnings.speaker: Adam Robinson
key_learnings.caveat: He paraphrases the prior ending rather than reproducing it exactly. Its claim that persistence improves the odds of major success is motivational, not quantified evidence.

key_learnings.claim: For a difficult ending, he recommends asking Claude for five playful, emotionally rewarding options and selecting the one closest to the writer’s tone and style.
key_learnings.speaker: Adam Robinson
key_learnings.caveat: This is advice rather than an explicit account of a completed personal workflow. The dopamine language is rhetorical, not a measured neurological result.

key_learnings.claim: He connects LinkedIn content to a sales workflow: identify people visiting the company website, deliver their LinkedIn profiles to Slack, and contact them while the content remains fresh in their minds. He characterizes prior website visitors as especially warm leads.
key_learnings.speaker: Adam Robinson
key_learnings.caveat: This is a product promotion, also introduced at 00:03:44–00:04:00. No identification accuracy, conversion rate, implementation conditions, or evidence for the warmest-lead superlative is provided. The product name is captioned as “OurB2B.”

backstory_and_values.claim: Adam reports that his early posts advocated eliminating BDRs in B2B SaaS and framed the predictable-revenue model as no longer effective. He presents the resulting disagreement as an example of his willingness to challenge a familiar industry model.
backstory_and_values.speaker: Adam Robinson
backstory_and_values.caveat: This establishes a reported public position, not evidence that he eliminated a particular team or that every SaaS company’s BDR model had failed.

backstory_and_values.claim: He says he published a post about a Retention.com layoff after his executive team advised him against it. The post disclosed lost product-market fit and an inability to resolve churn for 18 months; he explains his decision as an effort to be honest with people facing similar problems.
backstory_and_values.speaker: Adam Robinson
backstory_and_values.caveat: The layoff and post dates, affected headcount, churn measure, and eventual outcome are not supplied. This is evidence of a specific decision and stated rationale, not an approved mission claim.

backstory_and_values.claim: Adam names Chris Walker as a reference for hooks and Nigel Thomas as a reference for templates, while saying he refers to his own previous posts for endings.
backstory_and_values.speaker: Adam Robinson
backstory_and_values.caveat: Names come from automatic captions. These references establish stated sources of writing technique, not shared experiences, endorsements, or an approved voice identity.

backstory_and_values.claim: He says one of his proudest post endings addressed bootstrappers with encouragement to remain in the game and keep building, while recognizing the role of time and luck.
backstory_and_values.speaker: Adam Robinson
backstory_and_values.caveat: This is a reported editorial preference and prior message. It does not establish a personal hardship biography or a guarantee that persistence produces success.

metrics_and_dates.claim: Adam’s LinkedIn post performance: he reports dozens of posts reaching 100,000, 500,000, or more impressions.
metrics_and_dates.speaker: Adam Robinson
metrics_and_dates.caveat: Historical achievement claim as of publication on 2026-04-16; individual post dates, exact counts, and analytics are absent. The spoken unit is impressions, whereas the title says views.

metrics_and_dates.claim: Adam’s LinkedIn audience: he reports reaching 150,000 followers over the preceding three years.
metrics_and_dates.speaker: Adam Robinson
metrics_and_dates.caveat: Presented as current at recording/publication. The three-year period is relative to the statement; exact start and measurement dates are not supplied.

metrics_and_dates.speaker: Adam Robinson
metrics_and_dates.caveat: Presented as an achieved level by recording/publication, not a target. The transcript does not name the company or explicitly state the currency; the dollar notation is contextual. ARR is not revenue collected, profit, or cash. His causal attribution to LinkedIn is unverified.

metrics_and_dates.speaker: Adam Robinson
metrics_and_dates.caveat: No dataset, denominator definition, or measurement period is given; treat this as rhetorical emphasis rather than a platform statistic.

metrics_and_dates.speaker: Adam Robinson
metrics_and_dates.caveat: These dates belong to his provocative argument. They are not verified historical boundaries, and the date of the original post is unspecified.

metrics_and_dates.claim: Reaction to Adam’s BDR posts: he describes half the readers as agreeing and the other half as strongly disagreeing.
metrics_and_dates.speaker: Adam Robinson
metrics_and_dates.caveat: Likely an approximate description of polarization; no audience count, survey, or analytics supports a literal 50/50 split.

metrics_and_dates.speaker: Adam Robinson
metrics_and_dates.caveat: Historical duration, not a churn rate. No calendar endpoints, customer-versus-revenue churn definition, layoff headcount, or current churn result is supplied.

metrics_and_dates.speaker: Adam Robinson
metrics_and_dates.caveat: Promotional price and setup-time claims at publication, repeated at 00:06:50–00:07:15. No plan limits or measured installation results are given, and the captioned product spelling is uncertain.

metrics_and_dates.speaker: Adam Robinson
metrics_and_dates.caveat: Introduced as an example; do not record these conversations as an actual Adam achievement or research activity.

metrics_and_dates.claim: An unnamed business associated with Adam: he says a recurring personal hook is that he bootstrapped to $20 million ARR in three and a half years.
metrics_and_dates.speaker: Adam Robinson
metrics_and_dates.caveat: A claimed historical achievement, with no company name, calendar endpoints, or indication that this remains current ARR. Currency is not explicitly spoken. Do not equate it with the opening $8 million ARR claim or treat ARR as profit, cash, or recognized revenue.

metrics_and_dates.claim: Promoted LinkedIn course: Adam advertises a free course framed around growing from zero to 100,000 followers.
metrics_and_dates.speaker: Adam Robinson
metrics_and_dates.caveat: This is a course promise or scope, not a documented student achievement, guaranteed outcome, or a replacement for his separate 150,000-follower self-report.

tensions_and_corrections: The opening claim of more than $8 million ARR and the later $20 million ARR bootstrapping claim have unspecified company identities and dates. They may concern different businesses or periods; the transcript does not resolve the relationship.
The title uses views, but Adam describes LinkedIn impressions. Preserve the spoken measurement rather than treating the terms as interchangeable.
His advice to disclose uncomfortable truths includes an explicit boundary: investor-backed founders may have less latitude. It should not become a blanket recommendation for unrestricted disclosure.
He favors polarization within credibility limits and warns that excessively extreme positions can cause readers to dismiss the author.

He discourages generic engagement requests at the end of posts, yet includes direct product and course calls to action in this video. The source addresses different formats and does not establish opposition to all calls to action.
The body should contain an actionable takeaway, while the final line should create a feeling. These are distinct roles in his framework, not necessarily conflicting instructions.
Claims about fewer than 1% of creators, a half-and-half audience reaction, algorithm behavior, and the warmest possible leads are unsupported generalizations or approximations.
The product name appears as “OurB2B” in automatic captions. No external check was performed, so the spelling remains unresolved.
No explicit change of mind is narrated. The failed product-market-fit period is a business difficulty, not sufficient evidence of a broader reversal in Adam’s beliefs.
